blocks.body:
## The frozen judge is useful for screening, not autonomous enforcement

The final `gpt-4o-mini` judge agreed with human labels on **37 of 39 held-out traces (94.87%)**. It achieved **96.30% TPR** and **91.67% TNR**. The two errors show that the model can both miss a visible identifier and incorrectly attribute earlier trace identifiers to the final answer. Use it to prioritize human review, not as the sole policy gate.

## A shorter evidence-first prompt fixed the development miss

v0 and v1 each agreed on 38 of 39 development traces. v2 required the critique to inventory candidate identifiers from the complete last assistant block before applying the audience boundary; it reached 39 of 39 without introducing a development regression.

## Held-out performance remained strong but not perfect

The frozen prompt produced 26 true Pass decisions, 11 true Fail decisions, one false Fail, and one false Pass. The exact confusion counts are more useful than accuracy alone because false Passes represent missed leaks while false Fails create unnecessary human review.

## Both final errors were evidence-location failures

The false Pass overlooked `cw-returns` in a merchant-facing final reply. The false Fail claimed `cw-returns` and `cw-cancellations` appeared in a shopper-facing final reply that contained neither. The decision boundary was clear; the model failed to reliably isolate the final answer from the surrounding trace.

## Scope and metric definitions

The selected failure mode asks whether a shopper- or merchant-facing final reply exposes an unrequested raw internal policy identifier. **Pass is the positive class.** TPR is the fraction of human Pass labels reproduced as Pass; TNR is the fraction of human Fail labels reproduced as Fail. The fixed data comprised 19 training, 39 development, and 39 test conversations.

## Validation design protected the test from tuning

Four training-only examples shaped each prompt. Development results supported at most two revisions. v2 was selected and frozen before one held-out test run with the same model. Wilson intervals quantify uncertainty. Exact tables are used instead of a chart because three prompt versions and four confusion cells are clearer as audit-ready values than plotted marks.

## Small Fail counts keep uncertainty material

Test TPR has a 95% Wilson interval of **81.72%–99.34%** and test TNR has an interval of **64.61%–98.51%**. Only 12 human Fail cases were available in the test split, so the 91.67% TNR point estimate should not be interpreted as a precise production guarantee. The test errors also demonstrate that structured critiques can be confidently wrong.

## Preserve v2 and keep a human in the loop

- Use the judge to rank or flag traces for human review.
- Review all flagged cases and sample judge Pass cases to catch missed leaks.
- Revalidate after model or prompt changes.
- For production, consider a deterministic extractor that isolates the final assistant block before the LLM applies the audience/request boundary.
- Record the homework video using one development disagreement, the final metrics, and this use decision.

## The remaining technical question is trace isolation

Would a deterministic final-answer extractor remove both observed error types while preserving the LLM's contextual judgment about audience and explicit requests? That hybrid design is the clearest next experiment, but it is outside the required HW5 scope.
